__
 
• **Khums** was a tax levied during the **Delhi Sultanate** period on the treasure or booty looted in wars.
 
• The term **Khums** literally means "one-fifth" in Arabic, and it refers to the Islamic principle of taxing one-fifth (20%) of the war booty.
 
• This tax was collected by the state and was utilized for administrative purposes, public welfare, and religious activities.
 
• The remaining four-fifths of the booty were distributed among the soldiers who participated in the battle, as per Islamic law.
 
• The practice of levying **Khums** was in line with the Islamic traditions followed by the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate, such as the Slave Dynasty, Khilji Dynasty, and Tughlaq Dynasty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kharaj:**

 
 
• Kharaj was a **land tax** imposed on agricultural produce during the Delhi Sultanate period.
 
• It was usually levied on non-Muslim cultivators and was a significant source of revenue for the state.
 
• The tax rate varied but was typically fixed at one-third of the total agricultural produce.
 
 
 
• **Jizyah:**
 
 
• Jizyah was a tax levied on **non-Muslims** (referred to as Dhimmis) for protection and exemption from military service.
 
• This tax was an important financial contribution made by non-Muslim subjects to the Islamic state.
 
• Jizyah was abolished by Akbar but reinstated by Aurangzeb during the Mughal period.
 
 
 
• **Zakat:**
 
 
• Zakat is a **form of almsgiving** and one of the Five Pillars of Islam.
 
• It was a mandatory charitable contribution levied on Muslims, typically amounting to 2.5% of one’s wealth.
 
• Zakat was used for social welfare and assistance to the poor and needy.

• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** was given the title "**The Father of the Indian Unrest**" by the British colonial rulers due to his revolutionary ideas and activities in the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• This title was coined by the British writer and historian **Valentine Chirol** in his book titled "Indian Unrest" published in the early 20th century.
 
• Tilak’s strong opposition to British rule and his call for **Swaraj (self-rule)** resonated strongly among Indians, making him a prominent leader in the freedom movement.
 
• He played a crucial role in the **extremist faction** of the Indian National Congress, advocating for direct confrontation with colonial authorities rather than moderate dialogue.
 
• His famous statement, "**Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it**," became a rallying cry for Indian independence.

• **About Bal Gangadhar Tilak:**

 
 
• He was born on **23 July 1856** in Ratnagiri, Maharashtra.
 
• Tilak was one of the **earliest leaders of the Indian independence movement** and is often referred to as one of the "Lal-Bal-Pal" trio, along with Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal.
 
• He founded two nationalist newspapers, **Kesari (in Marathi)** and **The Mahratta (in English)**, which were instrumental in spreading anti-British sentiments.
 
• He was also a scholar of Indian culture and wrote extensively on the **Bhagavad Gita** and other Indian scriptures.
 
 
 
• **Other Titles and Contributions:**
 
 
• Despite the British calling him "The Father of the Indian Unrest," Tilak was also referred to as **"Lokmanya,"** meaning "accepted by the people as their leader."
 
• He introduced the **Ganesh Chaturthi** festival as a public event to unite people and instill a sense of nationalism.
 
• He was a key figure in the **Home Rule Movement** in 1916, which aimed to attain self-governance within the British Empire.
 
 
 
• **Context of the Title:**

• The mission aims at ensuring **functional tap water connections** to every household in **India's rural areas**.

questions.question: As of June 2025, how many Ramsar site are there in India?

The correct answer is __**91**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Ramsar Sites** are wetlands of international importance designated under the **Ramsar Convention**, an international treaty signed in **1971** in Ramsar, Iran. These sites are essential for biodiversity conservation and sustainable development.
 
• As of **June 2025**, **India has 91 Ramsar sites**, covering a total area of about **20,758.19 square kilometers**. These sites play a critical role in maintaining ecological balance.
 
• India is one of the contracting parties to the Ramsar Convention since **1982** and has been proactive in identifying and designating wetlands of ecological significance.
 
• The most recent additions to the list include wetlands like **Sakhya Sagar** in Madhya Pradesh and **Pala Wetland** in Mizoram, recognized for their biodiversity and ecological significance.
 
• India has the largest number of Ramsar sites in South Asia, demonstrating its commitment to wetland conservation and sustainable management practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Features of Ramsar Sites:**

 
 
• Wetlands provide critical ecosystem services such as **flood control, groundwater replenishment, and climate regulation**.
 
• They serve as habitats for a wide variety of **flora and fauna, including migratory birds**, amphibians, and aquatic species.
 
• Many Ramsar sites in India are culturally significant and are linked to the livelihoods of local communities.
 
 
 
• **Notable Ramsar Sites in India:**
 
 
• **Sundarbans Wetland** in West Bengal: It is the largest tidal halophytic mangrove forest in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
• **Chilika Lake** in Odisha: Asia's largest brackish water lagoon, known for its rich biodiversity and as a significant bird sanctuary.
 
• **Loktak Lake** in Manipur: Famous for its floating phumdis (heterogeneous masses of vegetation) and biodiversity.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Wetland Conservation:**
 
 
• Wetlands act as **natural water purifiers** by filtering pollutants from water.
 
• They are significant for **carbon sequestration**, helping mitigate climate change.
 
• Wetlands support sustainable livelihoods by providing resources like fish, fodder, and water for agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Ramsar Convention:**
 
 
• The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands is an international treaty adopted in **1971** to conserve and sustainably use wetlands.
 
• It emphasizes the "wise use" of wetlands, which involves maintaining their ecological character through sustainable practices.
 
• India is one of the **173 contracting parties** to the convention as of 2025.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Criteria for Ramsar Site Designation:**

 
 
• The site should support vulnerable, endangered, or critically endangered species.
 
• It should be a habitat for flora and fauna during critical stages of their life cycle.
 
• The site must play a significant role in maintaining the biological diversity of the region.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Wetland Conservation:**
 
 
• Threats like **urbanization, pollution, and encroachment** have led to the degradation of wetlands.
 
• Climate change impacts, such as altered rainfall patterns and rising temperatures, threaten wetland ecosystems.
 
• Efforts like community participation and government initiatives are crucial for wetland restoration and management.

questions.question: The first temple-building activity in India began during the rule of which dynasty?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gupta Dynasty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Gupta Dynasty** (circa 3rd to 6th century CE) is credited with initiating the first significant temple-building activity in India. Temples built during this period were primarily dedicated to **Hindu deities**, such as Vishnu, Shiva, and Shakti.
 
• The early Gupta temples were typically made of **brick and stone**, showcasing the transition from wood-based structures to more durable materials. This marked the beginning of India's rich temple architecture tradition.
 
• Examples of Gupta temple architecture include the **Dashavatara Temple** in Deogarh and the **Durga Temple** in Aihole. These temples featured simple designs, flat roofs, and intricate carvings that later evolved into more complex structures.
 
• The Gupta Dynasty is often referred to as the **"Golden Age of India"** due to its advancements in art, architecture, literature, and science. Temple-building was an integral part of this cultural resurgence.
 
• The temples built during the Gupta period laid the foundation for the development of **Nagara, Dravidian, and Vesara styles** of temple architecture, which flourished in later centuries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gupta Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Gupta Empire ruled over large parts of India between the **3rd and 6th centuries CE**.
 
• It is known for its significant contributions to **Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism**, and its promotion of Sanskrit literature.
 
• Key rulers included **Chandragupta I, Samudragupta**, and **Chandragupta II**, who patronized arts, culture, and temple-building projects.
 
 
 
• **Temple Architecture during Gupta Era:**
 
 
• The temples were small and modest in size but introduced key architectural features like **garbhagriha (sanctum sanctorum)** and **shikhara (spire).**
 
• They primarily used **stone and terracotta** for construction, replacing earlier wooden structures.
 
• The Dashavatara Temple in Deogarh is one of the earliest examples of a **Nagara-style temple** with a square sanctum and intricate carvings.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Explained:**
 
 
• **Ahom Kingdom:**
 
 
• The Ahom Kingdom (1228–1826 CE) was located in present-day Assam and is known for its unique architecture, such as the **Rang Ghar**, but it is not associated with the origins of temple-building in India.
 
 
 
• **Vijayanagara Empire:**
 
 
• The Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE) in South India is famous for its **Dravidian-style temples**, such as the **Virupaksha Temple**, but it came much later than the Gupta period.
 
 
 
• **Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty (8th–11th century CE) significantly contributed to temple architecture, especially in **North India**, but their temple-building activities were inspired by earlier Gupta structures.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Gupta Temples:**
 
 
• The architectural principles established during the Gupta period influenced temple-building activities across India for centuries.
 
• The cultural and religious importance of temples grew during and after the Gupta era, making them centers of devotion, art, and learning.

• During this dance, women carry **decorated brass vessels** (often illuminated with oil lamps or candles) on their heads, which adds a spiritual and celebratory element to the performance.
 
• The dance is accompanied by traditional **Punjabi folk songs** that are sung collectively, often humorously teasing the bride, groom, or their families.
 
• ‘**Jaago**’ reflects the rich cultural heritage of Punjab and is deeply rooted in the traditions and customs of Punjabi weddings.

• **Punjab’s Cultural Significance:**

 
 
• Punjab is known for its vibrant culture, which includes traditional dances like **Bhangra**, **Giddha**, and **Jaago**.
 
• The state has a rich tradition of folk music and dance, which are often performed during festivals, harvests, and other significant occasions.
 
• ‘Jaago’ is particularly significant as it blends **community participation** with a sense of celebration and joy.
 
 
 
• **Other Traditional Dances of Punjab:**
 
 
• **Bhangra:** A high-energy dance performed mostly by men during harvest festivals such as **Baisakhi**.
 
• **Giddha:** A lively women’s dance that involves clapping and singing boliyan (folk couplets).
 
• **Sammi:** A less well-known dance performed by women in rural areas of Punjab, often characterized by slow, graceful movements.
 
 
 
• **Significance of ‘Jaago’:**
 
 
• ‘Jaago’ is symbolic of **community unity and celebration** during weddings, where everyone is invited to join the revelry.
 
• The lit candles or lamps in the brass vessels signify **light and hope** for the new couple's journey ahead.
 
 
 
• **Traditional Elements:**
 
 
• The decorative vessels used in ‘Jaago’ are called **“chajj”** and are adorned with flowers, mirrors, and colorful threads.
 
• The folk songs sung during ‘Jaago’ are often humorous, adding a playful element to the occasion.

• **Jharkhand:** Known for tribal dances such as **Chhau** and **Paika**, which are distinct from Punjab’s ‘Jaago’ dance.
 
• **Odisha:** Famous for **Odissi dance** and folk dances like **Dalkhai** and **Chhau**. These are classical and tribal in nature.
 
• **Maharashtra:** Popular for **Lavani** and **Koli** dances, showcasing the cultural essence of the state’s fisherfolk and rural communities.

questions.question:
Which of the following organ can be donated while the donor is alive?

I. Part of a liver

II. Kidney
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Living organ donation** allows healthy individuals to donate certain organs or tissues while they are alive to save or enhance the lives of others. This is regulated under strict medical guidelines and ethical considerations.
 
• Part of a liver can be donated by a living donor. The liver has a unique ability to regenerate, making it possible for a portion of the liver to be transplanted while the donor’s liver regrows to its normal size. ***Hence, statement I is correct.***
 
• A kidney can be donated by a living donor. Humans typically have two kidneys, and one kidney is sufficient for a donor to live a healthy life while the donated kidney can save the life of the recipient. ***Hence, statement II is correct.***
 
• Living organ donation is strictly regulated to ensure the safety of both the donor and the recipient. It requires comprehensive medical evaluations and legal consent processes.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both I and II.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Organ Donation:**

 
 
• Organ donation refers to the process of donating organs or tissues from a donor to a recipient. It can be done either after death (cadaveric donation) or by living donors.
 
• Living donors can donate organs like kidneys, part of the liver, or tissues such as bone marrow, provided they meet strict medical criteria.
 
• Organ donations save lives, especially in cases of chronic organ failure such as kidney or liver failure.
 
 
 
• **Liver Donation:**
 
 
• The liver is the only organ in the human body capable of regenerating itself. This allows living donors to donate a portion of their liver, which regrows to its normal size in both the donor and the recipient.
 
• Liver donation typically involves removing either the right or left lobe of the liver, depending on the size and needs of the recipient.
 
• Regeneration usually takes place within a few months of donation.
 
 
 
• **Kidney Donation:**
 
 
• Kidneys are vital for filtering waste and maintaining fluid balance in the body. Living individuals with healthy kidney function can donate one kidney.
 
• A kidney transplant is often the best treatment for end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or chronic kidney failure.
 
• Donors undergo extensive medical evaluations to ensure their remaining kidney can sustain normal kidney function.
 
 
 
• **Legal and Ethical Guidelines:**
 
 
• Organ donation is regulated under laws such as the **Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994,** in India, which ensures ethical practices and prohibits organ trafficking.
 
• Donors must give informed consent, and medical professionals must ensure donors are not coerced or exploited.
 
• Both donor and recipient undergo psychological and medical evaluations to ensure a safe and ethical transplant process.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Eligibility for Living Donation:**

 
 
• Donors must be in good physical and mental health, typically between the ages of **18 and 60 years**.
 
• They must undergo rigorous medical tests, including blood tests, imaging scans, and psychological assessments.
 
• Living donors are often family members or close relatives of the recipient to reduce the risk of organ rejection.
 
 
 
• **Statistics:**
 
 
• Globally, living organ donation accounts for a significant portion of transplants. For example, in **India**, about **90% of kidney transplants** come from living donors.
 
• Countries like the **United States** and **South Korea** also see high rates of living donation, particularly for kidney and liver transplants.
 
 
 
• **Awareness Campaigns:**
 
 
• Initiatives like **National Organ Donation Day** (celebrated annually on **27th November** in India) aim to educate the public about the life-saving benefits of organ donation.
